open-question.question: Where is the banner SVG committed, and how does it reach the three host landing pages, given that a host README's relative path resolves only to a file its own host tree carries and that the build copies only the root LICENSE into every tree: is a copy carried in each host tree and referenced by a relative path, or do the host READMEs reference a single file in the source repository by absolute URL? If each tree carries a copy, where does it come from: a file kept by hand in each of the three definition directories under scripts/hosts/, or a build change that copies one shared file into every tree?
open-question.alternative: Each host tree carries its own copy of the SVG, referenced by a relative path from its README. Each copy is a file kept by hand in its definition directory (scripts/hosts/claude/, scripts/hosts/antigravity/, scripts/hosts/codex/), which the build picks up as a template and renders to the same relative path at the tree root. The root README references a fourth hand-kept copy at a root location (for example an assets/ directory) by a relative path. There is no build change, and the four copies are kept identical by hand, as the three traffic-badges.yml copies are. It needs no change to scripts/build_hosts.py. It uses the build's existing template channel and the repository's existing practice for a file every tree needs. Every page loads its banner from its own repository, so no page depends on another repository or a URL staying valid. Four copies must be kept byte-identical by hand, and nothing checks that they agree: --check compares each tree only with its own definition directory. The work doubles if the light-and-dark question settles on separate variants, and it multiplies further if the source-of-truth question settles on a generator script that writes every copy. Each SVG is UTF-8, so the build rewrites {{VERSION}}/{{NAME}} in it and runs the tree checks on it. Each copy also lands in the installed plugin for Claude Code and Antigravity, and adds a file to every host's trigger set for the host suite.

alternative.id: Hand-kept copies, root reads a host tree

open-question.alternative: Each host tree carries its own copy, kept by hand in its definition directory and referenced by a relative path from its README, as in the previous option. The root README keeps no copy of its own. It references one host's rendered copy by a relative path (for example hosts/claude/banner.svg). There is no build change, and three copies are kept identical by hand. It has one hand-kept copy fewer than the four-copy layout and still needs no build change. Every host page still loads its banner from its own repository. The source repository's landing page depends on build output in one host's tree, which the repository otherwise treats as never hand-edited and as belonging to that host. If that host's tree is renamed, restructured, or dropped, the root banner breaks with no check catching it. The three host copies still have nothing checking that they agree, and they still land in the installed plugin for Claude Code and Antigravity.

One SVG is committed once in the source repository at a root location (for example an assets/ directory). The root README references it by a relative path. scripts/build_hosts.py is changed to copy that one file into every host tree at the tree root, beside the README, byte for byte as it copies the root LICENSE. Each host README references its tree's copy by a relative path. The build's tests are extended to cover the new copy. There is a single file to edit, and every host tree's copy is derived from it. --check then guarantees that the committed trees match the source byte for byte, and every page still loads its banner from its own repository. That gives one source with no hand synchronisation and no dependence on a remote URL. It changes the host build, which today copies exactly one shared root file, so it adds a code change, a test, and a new build input to a mission otherwise limited to README content. The copy lands in the installed plugin for Claude Code and Antigravity. If the light-and-dark question settles on separate variants, the build must copy every variant.

One SVG is committed once in the source repository at a root location, and no host tree carries a copy. The root README references the file by a relative path. Each host README template references the same file by an absolute raw.githubusercontent.com URL on the uHappyLogic/gurita main branch, the way the traffic badges already reference SVGs on the traffic-data branch. There is no build change. It is the smallest change: one file, no copies, and no build change. It follows the absolute-URL pattern every image on the four pages already uses. A later change to the banner reaches all three host pages as soon as it is pushed, with no release. Published host pages track whatever main holds, so they stop matching their release. A banner edit shows on every host page before it ships, and moving, renaming, or deleting the file on main breaks the banner on every host page, including pages left by past releases. The installed plugin's README also shows the banner only when online.

alternative.id: Absolute URL pinned to release tag

open-question.alternative: One SVG is committed once in the source repository at a root location, and no host tree carries a copy. The root README references the file by a relative path. Each host README template references it by an absolute raw.githubusercontent.com URL on uHappyLogic/gurita at the release tag, written as {{VERSION}}, which the build already fills in host README templates. Each published host page therefore shows the banner as it stood at its own release. There is no build change. There is one file, no copies, and no build change, and each host page is still frozen to its release. A later edit, move, or deletion on main never changes or breaks a page already published. The release procedure already pushes the bare MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH tag before it publishes the distribution repositories. The URL resolves only once the tag that names it has been pushed and holds the file. Until a release that includes the banner, the rendered hosts/<host>/README.md on main points at a tag (2.0.0 today) that has no banner, so it shows a broken image when browsed in the source repository. The banner also cannot be fixed on a published page without a new release. The installed plugin's README shows the banner only when online.

open-question.question: What is the source of truth for the banner: is the SVG file written and edited directly, or is the character art kept as a plain-text drawing from which a committed script generates the SVG, the repository holding no such script today?
open-question.alternative: The committed SVG is the only source of truth. It is written and later edited by hand as SVG, with the character art, its colours, and its layout held only inside the file. No plain-text drawing is kept beside it and no generator script is committed. However its first version comes to be written, every later change is an edit of the SVG itself. One artifact and nothing to keep in step with it. The repository gains no script, no new dependency, and no command a later editor must know to run. This matches how the README templates and the three traffic-workflow copies are kept today, as hand-edited files. Changing the art means editing XML: positions, row elements, and characters that must be escaped (a literal & or < in the art becomes an entity). A diff of the art is then unreadable as a picture, so a reviewer cannot see what a change does to the drawing. Whether direct editing is practical at all depends on the Character rendering in SVG question's axis: with text elements it is tedious, and with glyphs converted to outline paths it is effectively impossible by hand.

A plain-text drawing of the arms, with whatever colour mapping it needs, is committed as the source of truth. A new standalone script under scripts/ is committed beside it, run by hand like set_version.py, and reads the drawing to write the SVG. The generated SVG is committed as derived output, never hand-edited, and is regenerated whenever the drawing changes. The art stays editable and reviewable as a picture in plain text, and the SVG is reproducible from it. A redraw, a palette change, or a switch in how the characters are rendered is one edit plus one rerun, not a rewrite of the XML. Generated output that is committed and never hand-edited is the pattern the repository already follows for hosts/. The repository gains a script that must be written, kept working, and remembered whenever the art changes. Nothing ties the committed SVG to the drawing, so the two can drift silently unless a guard is added. Whether such a guard exists is the Permanent banner check question's axis, not this one's. The script also has to take a position on the Character rendering in SVG and Light and dark themes questions' axes, which becomes code to change if either answer changes.

alternative.id: Drawing rendered by the host build

open-question.alternative: The plain-text drawing is committed as the source of truth, and scripts/build_hosts.py itself renders the SVG from it as part of every host build. The generated file is written into each host tree and committed there as build output, with --check comparing it against a fresh render like every other file in the tree. The root README's copy is produced by the same rendering code rather than by a separate script. The drawing and the host copies of the SVG cannot drift unnoticed: the existing --check gate catches any difference on every push, in CI, and in the release pre-flight. There is no separate command for anyone to remember to run. Banner-specific rendering moves into the one generic host build, which today renders templates and has no host-specific or content-specific code. The build writes nothing outside hosts/, so the root README's copy falls outside --check unless the build's output set is widened. This option only works if the Banner delivery to host pages question has each host tree carry its own copy, rather than having the READMEs reference one file by absolute URL.

The plain-text drawing is committed beside the SVG as a readable reference to the art. The SVG is produced from it once, by hand or by a one-off conversion that is not committed. From then on the SVG is the file the READMEs use, and a later change is made to both by hand. No generator script lives in the repository. Reviewers can read the art as text in the repository and in diffs, and no script has to be maintained. Two hand-kept artifacts describe one picture with no mechanical link between them, so they drift as soon as one is edited without the other. The SVG is then the real source of truth in practice, and the text file a record that may already be out of date. A redraw also means repeating or reconstructing the conversion that was never kept.

open-question.question: How are the banner's characters drawn inside the SVG, given that GitHub loads no external font for an SVG shown as an image and a text element is drawn in whatever font the viewer's system supplies: as text elements relying on a system monospace font stack, as text with a font embedded in the file, or as glyph outlines converted to paths?
open-question.alternative: Each row of the art is a text element (or a tspan per row) with whitespace preserved, its font-family a system monospace stack such as ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Menlo, Consolas, DejaVu Sans Mono, monospace. No font is embedded and no character carries its own position, so column alignment comes from whatever monospace font the viewer's system supplies. It is the smallest and simplest file. A plain-text drawing maps onto it line for line, it needs no tool beyond a text editor or the stdlib, and it adds no font licence to the repository. The look varies from viewer to viewer. Glyph shapes, advance widths, and line metrics differ between Menlo, Consolas, DejaVu Sans Mono, and the rest, so the art's width, and the point where the curling arms meet the bottom edge, shift against a fixed viewBox, and the image may clip or leave gaps. Any check done on one machine says little about another. If the art uses Unicode box-drawing, block, or braille glyphs (the Art character set question), a system font may lack them and substitute a proportional fallback that breaks the columns.

Text elements in a system monospace stack, as above, but every character is placed on a fixed grid regardless of the font's own advance widths. Each row is a tspan with an explicit x list, one coordinate per column, or a textLength with lengthAdjust fitted to the row's grid width. No font is embedded. It keeps the small, licence-free text file but guarantees the columns line up, and that the art fills the viewBox exactly, whichever monospace font the viewer gets. This removes the main failure of relying on font metrics. Glyph shapes, weights, and vertical metrics still differ per system, so the art never looks the same everywhere, and a missing glyph still falls back to another font. The per-character coordinate lists make the file impractical to write or edit by hand, so this option effectively needs a generator, which depends on how the Banner source of truth question is settled.

Text elements whose font-family names a font defined by an @font-face rule in the SVG's own style element. The rule's src is a base64 data URI of one complete monospace font file under a licence that permits embedding and redistribution, for example the SIL Open Font License. The font is not subset, and the system stack is kept only as a fallback. Every viewer draws the art in the same chosen font with known metrics, because a data URI is not an external load. The base64 encoding needs only the Python stdlib, so no new dependency enters the tooling project. A complete monospace font runs to tens or hundreds of kilobytes, inflated by a third in base64. That weight sits in every committed copy and in each README page load, and the copies multiply if Banner delivery to host pages puts one in each host tree. It also brings a third-party font and its licence text into the repository, and it relies on the image renderer honouring an embedded data-URI font, which needs checking under Rendered look verification.

Text elements, as with the whole font, but the @font-face data URI holds a subset of a licence-compatible monospace font cut down to the glyphs the art actually uses. The subset is produced with a font tool such as fonttools' pyftsubset, and the system stack is kept as a fallback. It gives the same consistent rendering as embedding the whole font at a file size of a few kilobytes, so the banner stays light in every copy and on every page load while the art remains live text. It needs a subsetting tool that the repository does not hold today (its one tooling dependency is PyYAML), and the subset must be rebuilt whenever the art gains a new character. Without a committed generator that becomes a manual, easily forgotten step, which ties it to the Banner source of truth question. It also carries the third-party font licence, and the same reliance on the renderer honouring a data-URI font.

The SVG holds no text element. Each character of the art is drawn as its glyph outline, taken from a chosen licence-compatible monospace font and placed on the character grid as path data, either inline per character or as one symbol per distinct glyph reused through use elements. The colours are applied as fills. It looks identical in every renderer and on every system, depending on no font being present or honoured. This rules out metric drift, missing glyphs, and data-URI font support in one step, whatever the Art character set question decides. The file is no longer text that can be read or edited as character art. Every change to the drawing means converting it again, with a font tool such as fonttools or an editor like Inkscape that the repository does not hold, so in practice it needs a generator (see Banner source of truth). The path data is larger than plain text unless glyphs are reused through use elements, and the art is not selectable as text.

open-question.question: Which characters may the banner's art use: only the printable 7-bit ASCII characters, or also Unicode characters such as box-drawing, block, or braille glyphs?
open-question.alternative: The art uses only the 95 printable 7-bit ASCII characters (U+0020 to U+007E): the arms' curls are built from characters such as / \ | ( ) _ ~ ' . , o and similar, and no character outside that range appears anywhere in the drawing. It keeps the goal's "ASCII art" literal, and every monospace font a viewer's system can supply covers this range with one uniform advance width, so the columns stay aligned and no glyph falls back to a different font whichever way the characters end up drawn in the SVG; the drawing also stays a plain-text file any editor or script handles without encoding concerns. Curves made of slashes, brackets, and underscores are coarse and stair-stepped, so arms curling up from the bottom edge read less smoothly and need more columns and rows to look organic, and the colour palette can only tint thin line characters, with no solid or shaded areas to carry it.

alternative.id: ASCII plus box-drawing and block glyphs

open-question.alternative: The art may use the printable ASCII characters plus the Unicode Box Drawing (U+2500 to U+257F) and Block Elements (U+2580 to U+259F) ranges, for example rounded arcs such as ╭ ╮ ╰ ╯, lines, and the shade and fill blocks ░ ▒ ▓ █; braille and every other Unicode range stay excluded. Rounded arc glyphs give the curling arms smooth turns that slashes cannot, and the shade blocks let the violet and grey-blue palette fill and grade the arms' bodies, while both ranges are carried by the common monospace fonts (Menlo, Consolas, DejaVu Sans Mono and the like) at the same cell width as ASCII. The art is no longer ASCII in the strict sense the goal's wording names, and its alignment holds only where the glyphs are drawn at a uniform width: whether that is guaranteed depends on the sibling question of how the characters are rendered in the SVG, since a viewer font lacking a glyph substitutes another font whose width and baseline may differ, and block glyphs can show hairline seams between rows.

The art may use any Unicode character the drawing calls for, braille patterns (U+2800 to U+28FF) included alongside ASCII, box-drawing, and block glyphs, with no range excluded. Braille patterns give each character cell a 2 by 4 grid of dots, so the arms' curves and suckers can be drawn at close to pixel resolution, giving the smoothest and most detailed silhouette any character set allows. Braille and the less common ranges have the weakest monospace font coverage, so this option is viable only if the sibling question on character rendering settles on a method that does not depend on the viewer's fonts; dense braille also reads as a dithered picture rather than as a drawing made of characters, drifting furthest from the "ASCII art" the goal names, and the plain-text source becomes hard to read or edit by hand.

open-question.question: How does the banner handle GitHub's light and dark page themes, no README today using a picture element or a theme-specific image variant: one image with a transparent background whose colours must read on both page backgrounds, one image with its own filled background, or separate light and dark variants selected per theme?
open-question.alternative: One SVG with no background fill, so the page shows through, its violet and grey-blue colours picked to keep enough contrast on both GitHub's white light background and its near-black dark background. The README holds one plain image reference and no theme selection markup. One file and one image reference per README. It works the same in every renderer, including the host READMEs installed with the plugin and read outside GitHub, and it blends into whichever page it sits on. Only mid-luminance colours read on both backgrounds, so the palette is pushed toward middle tones. Fine character strokes lose contrast on one theme or the other, and the darker shades the diagram uses (#581c87, #475569) nearly vanish on the dark page. This option stands or falls with the colour values the palette question picks.

One SVG that paints its own dark, terminal-like background rectangle behind the art, so the colours are drawn against a fixed backdrop whatever the page theme. The README holds one plain image reference and no theme selection markup. The colours are tuned against one known background, so the art looks the same everywhere. A dark backdrop suits character art drawn in violet and grey-blue, and the setup stays one file with one reference. On the light theme the banner is a heavy dark block at the very top of the page, which visually outweighs the badges and title below it. Its edges show as a hard rectangle on both themes unless the corners are softened.

One SVG that paints its own light background rectangle (white or a pale tint) behind the art, so the colours are drawn against a fixed light backdrop whatever the page theme. The README holds one plain image reference and no theme selection markup. It matches the root README's Mermaid diagram, which also sits on white fills with violet and slate strokes. On the default light theme it is almost seamless, and the setup stays one file with one reference. On the dark theme the banner is a bright block that glares at the top of an otherwise dark page, the most visible spot. This is the theme where a filled background is noticed most.

Two SVGs, one coloured for the light theme and one for the dark, both with transparent backgrounds. Each README wraps them in a `` element whose `` selects the dark file and whose fallback `` shows the light one. This is GitHub's documented way of serving theme-specific images, and it follows the theme the viewer has set on GitHub. Each variant gets the full contrast range for its own background, and any renderer that ignores the source still shows the fallback image. There are two files to draw, colour, and keep in step, and every README needs more markup. If the delivery question puts a copy in each host tree, that means six SVG copies instead of three. If the source-of-truth question leaves the SVG hand-edited, every change to the art is made twice.

Two SVGs, one coloured for the light theme and one for the dark, both with transparent backgrounds. Each README references both with plain image syntax, tagging the URLs with GitHub's `#gh-light-mode-only` and `#gh-dark-mode-only` fragments so GitHub hides whichever does not match the current theme. Each theme gets its own full-contrast colours using only plain Markdown image references, without any HTML element. The fragments are a GitHub-only convention that GitHub has replaced with the picture element in its documentation. Any other renderer, including a host README read from an installed plugin copy, shows both banners stacked. It also carries the same two-file maintenance cost as the picture-element option.

One SVG with a transparent background whose own embedded CSS uses an `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` rule to swap the art's colours. The README holds one plain image reference and no theme selection markup. One file and one reference still give per-theme colours. The theme logic stays inside the image, so every README and every host copy stays as simple as a single image. When the SVG is shown as an image, the browser resolves the media query from the operating system or browser colour preference, not from the theme chosen in GitHub's settings. A viewer whose GitHub theme differs from their system setting gets the wrong variant. Renderers that do not evaluate CSS in an SVG image fall back to the default colours.

One SVG with a transparent background whose colours are chosen for GitHub's default light page only. The dark theme gets whatever contrast those colours happen to have, and the README holds one plain image reference with no theme handling. It is the least work and the least to maintain: colours are tuned to one background, there is one file, and no markup beyond the image. Theme handling stays open for a later change if dark-theme readers complain. Viewers using the dark theme, a large share of GitHub users, may see the darker violet and slate strokes nearly disappear. The page's most prominent element would then look broken to them.

open-question.question: Which exact colour values make up the banner's violet and grey-blue palette: the values the root README's workflow diagram already uses (violet #9333ea and #581c87, slate #94a3b8 and #475569), or values chosen for the banner alone?
open-question.alternative: The banner uses exactly the four colours the root README's Mermaid diagram already uses for its violet and slate parts, and no other: violet #9333ea (the diagram's stroke) and deep violet #581c87 (its text), slate #94a3b8 (its lines) and #475569 (its borders), each assigned to parts of the arms (for example outline versus shading) by the drawing. The banner and the diagram on the root page share one palette with no new value to choose or justify, so the page reads as one design and the exact values are already recorded in the repository. The values were chosen for a diagram drawn on white fills, and the two dark tones (#581c87, #475569) lose most of their contrast on GitHub's dark page background, so this option holds up only if the banner's handling of themes (owned by the light and dark themes question) gives it a light background or a light-only variant; the matching also shows on the root page alone, the host READMEs carrying no diagram.

The banner uses only the two mid-tone diagram values, violet #9333ea and slate #94a3b8, one colour per palette half, and leaves out the diagram's dark text and border tones (#581c87, #475569). It stays strictly within values the page already uses while keeping only the two that remain legible on both a white and a near-black page, so it is the reuse option least dependent on how the banner handles themes. Two flat colours give the drawing little room for depth or shading between arms, and slate #94a3b8 is low in contrast on a white page, so the grey-blue parts read faintly in the light theme.

The banner takes its colours from the same violet and slate families the diagram draws on (the scale holding #faf5ff, #9333ea, and #581c87 on the violet side and #94a3b8 and #475569 on the slate side), but picks the shades for the banner itself, lighter or darker steps of those families included, as many as the drawing needs, the chosen hex values recorded in the requirements. The banner keeps the diagram's hues, so the root page stays visually related, while each shade can be chosen for legibility against whatever background the banner ends up on. New values have to be chosen and recorded now, before the art or its theme handling exists, and the banner matches the diagram only in hue, not value for value.

The banner uses a violet and grey-blue palette chosen for it alone, independent of the diagram's colour families (its own hex values, as many as the drawing needs), recorded in the requirements. The palette can be tuned wholly to the art and to how characters render at banner size, with no constraint inherited from a diagram designed for a different purpose. The root page would then carry two unrelated violets and two unrelated grey-blues a few lines apart, and the values are chosen with no anchor in anything the project already uses.

No exact values are recorded as a decision: the requirements keep only the goal's "violet and grey-blue palette", and the concrete hex values are chosen by whoever produces the drawing, at the time the SVG is made. The values are picked with the drawing and its rendering in hand, when legibility and look can actually be judged, rather than fixed in the abstract beforehand. Task completion has no recorded colour criterion to verify against, so the outcome rests entirely on the drawing's author and on whatever rendering check is made (owned by the drawing author and rendered look verification questions), and nothing records why the values were chosen.

open-question.question: How many arms does the banner show, the goal saying only "several": all eight of an octopus's arms, or a smaller number?
open-question.alternative: The banner shows exactly eight arms, every one of an octopus's arms, each curling up from the bottom edge, and the requirements record eight as a fixed count the drawing must meet. It carries the image the project already chose: ideas/gurita.md records that an octopus has eight arms and that "the plugin is the arms", so the banner states the full metaphor rather than a fragment of it, and a fixed count gives the drawing an objective criterion to be checked against. Eight curling arms side by side need many character columns to stay legible, so the art is either wide or crowded with arms too thin to curl; whether that fits depends on the column count and display width the banner-size question settles, and an eight-arm drawing is the hardest of the options to make read well in characters.

The banner shows a fixed number of arms below eight, chosen from three to five, framed as a view in which only some of the octopus's arms rise into the banner, and the requirements record the exact number the drawing must meet. Fewer arms leave each one room for a full, legible curl within a modest width, the reading the goal's "several" already suggests, while a recorded number still gives the drawing an objective criterion. It gives up the eight-arm image the naming draft rests on, so a viewer reads it as part of an octopus rather than the whole set of arms the plugin claims to be, and any number chosen in the range is arbitrary with no project fact to anchor it.

No arm count is recorded: the requirements keep the goal's "several", meaning more than two, and the number is settled when the character drawing is made, by whatever look reads best at the banner's size. The count follows from the drawing's actual space and legibility rather than being fixed before any art exists, so it never forces eight arms into too few columns or leaves an awkward gap with too few. The drawing has no countable criterion to be accepted against, so the number becomes whatever the drawer's judgment yields; that is acceptable only as far as the drawing-author-and-approval question puts a judge in place who can weigh it, and an unattended drawer may land on a count that reads as neither a deliberate eight nor a deliberate fragment.

open-question.question: What size is the banner, given that it sits above everything else on the page and pushes the badges and title down: how many character columns and rows does the art occupy, and at what width is the image displayed, the full width of the README column or a fixed narrower width?
open-question.alternative: The art is a wide, low strip of about 80 to 100 character columns by about 8 to 12 rows, so its aspect is roughly 4:1 to 6:1. It is displayed at the full width of the README column (an img width of 100%), which comes to about 800 to 900 pixels on a desktop repository page and shrinks with the column on narrow screens. The same grid and width apply to all four READMEs. At full desktop width it takes only about 150 to 220 pixels of height, so the badges and, in the root README, the traffic table and the title move down by little, while each character cell stays about 8 to 10 pixels wide, readable as a character. A dozen rows leaves little height for arms to curl up from the bottom edge, so the curls come out flat and the drawing reads more as a border than as arms. On a phone-width column the characters shrink to 3 or 4 pixels and read as texture. How many arms fit side by side depends on the arm count a sibling question settles.

The art is a fuller drawing of about 80 to 100 character columns by about 20 to 30 rows, an aspect of roughly 2:1 to 3:1, displayed at the full width of the README column (an img width of 100%), so about 300 to 450 pixels tall on a desktop page. The same grid and width apply to all four READMEs. It gives the arms room to rise from the bottom edge and curl back over, so the octopus image the tagline draws on is unmistakable and the banner is a clear visual opening of the page. Above the root README's badges and four-row traffic table it pushes the `# Gurita` title and tagline well down, likely below the first screen on a laptop, and on the host pages it takes more height than everything that follows the badges up to the pitch. A taller drawing is also more character work to draw and to check.

The art is a high-resolution grid of about 140 to 180 character columns by about 30 to 45 rows, displayed at the full width of the README column (an img width of 100%), so each character cell is about 5 to 6 pixels wide on a desktop page and the drawing is about 250 to 400 pixels tall. The fine grid allows smooth curls, tapering arm tips, and shading, so the arms look drawn rather than blocky. At that cell size the characters stop reading as characters and become shading, which loses the drawn-in-characters look the goal asks for, and on a phone they vanish into a grey wash. A 150-column drawing is also hard to edit and to review by eye. Whether density reads as texture depends on the character set a sibling question settles.

The art is a medium grid of about 50 to 70 character columns by about 12 to 18 rows, displayed centred at a fixed width narrower than the column, about 480 to 640 pixels, set by an explicit img width attribute inside a centred block like the badges' own `p align="center"`, and scaling down only where the column is narrower than that width. The same grid and width apply to all four READMEs. The banner's height is bounded at about 200 to 300 pixels on every desktop page whatever the window width, and centred it lines up with the centred badges and traffic table beneath it, so the page opening stays compact and consistent. Fewer columns give the arms less horizontal room, so several arms side by side have to be narrow or few, and a banner narrower than the column reads as a logo rather than a header. How many arms fit depends on the arm count a sibling question settles.

The SVG declares an intrinsic width and height computed from its grid at a fixed character cell matching README body text (about 16 pixels per row and roughly 8 to 10 pixels per column), the img carries no width attribute, and the image shows at that natural size, centred, with GitHub's image styling scaling it down only when the column is narrower. The grid is a medium one of about 60 to 80 columns by about 10 to 16 rows, so it shows at about 500 to 800 pixels wide and 160 to 260 pixels tall. The characters appear at the same size as the page's own text on every desktop page, so the art reads as character art rather than as a picture of it, and the displayed size follows from the drawing alone with no separate width to choose or keep in sync across four READMEs. The displayed width is no longer chosen: changing the drawing's column count changes how wide the banner shows, so the banner may end up neither full-width nor a deliberate narrower width, and its edge will not line up with anything else on the page.

No grid size or display width is fixed in the requirements now: whoever draws the art chooses the column and row count and the display width while drawing, constrained only by the goal, and the size is settled when the drawing is made rather than in this mission's decisions. The size can follow what the drawing actually needs once arms are on the grid, instead of a number fixed before anyone has tried to draw them. How far the banner pushes the badges and title down, the concern the question raises, is then decided by no recorded criterion, so an unattended run can ship a banner that buries the title, and the four READMEs may drift apart if each is sized separately. Its acceptability depends on who draws and approves the art, which a sibling question settles.

open-question.question: Who produces the character drawing of the arms, and what decides it is good enough to ship: does the executing agent draw it and accept it on its own judgment against criteria recorded in the requirements, does the agent draw it for the maintainer to approve before it lands in the READMEs, or does the maintainer supply the drawing?
open-question.alternative: The executing agent draws the character art itself during task completion. It accepts the drawing on its own judgment, checked against acceptance criteria written into requirements.md before tasks are derived, for example arms visibly curling upward from the bottom edge, the shapes readable as arms rather than noise, and no recognisable letters or words formed by accident. No maintainer review is held before the drawing lands in the four READMEs. The mission stays fully unattended through complete-all-tasks. The completion procedure derives its acceptance bar from requirements.md, so recorded criteria become checkable bullets in the Task-completion commit body rather than a judgment of taste left unstated. Taste criteria are hard to state so that an agent's self-check is meaningful. A drawing can pass every written criterion and still look poor, and the first human to see it is a visitor to the landing page. How much the criteria can say depends on axes sibling questions own (arm count, size, character set).

The executing agent draws the art and accepts it on its own judgment against the goal's wording alone ("several octopus arms curling up from the bottom edge"). No acceptance criteria are recorded beyond what other decisions already fix, and no maintainer review is held before it lands. Costs no extra decision work now and nothing during execution. The agent has the most freedom to find a drawing that works, rather than being held to criteria written before anyone has seen a draft. The completion bar for the drawing is whatever the agent writes for itself at run time, so "good enough" is not checkable against anything recorded. A weak drawing passes as easily as a strong one and ships unseen.

The executing agent draws the art, offering one draft or a few candidates, and the drawing lands in the READMEs only after the maintainer approves or picks one. The maintainer's verdict is the acceptance gate, with revisions requested until it passes. In the task list the drawing and its placement in the READMEs are separate tasks, with the maintainer's review between them. A human with taste sees the art before any landing page shows it. For a purely aesthetic deliverable at the top of every page, that is the one judgment no recorded criterion can stand in for. Breaks unattended execution: the completion runners return only DONE or FAILED and have no pause for approval, so complete-all-tasks has to stop at the review point and the maintainer has to resume it by hand. Each rejected draft costs a round trip and a task of its own.

The executing agent draws the art and lands it in the READMEs on its own judgment against recorded criteria, unattended. The maintainer then reviews the result on main afterwards, before it matters, and any correction is entered as a follow-up task or made by reverting the commit. Keeps the task run unattended while still putting a human eye on the art. The review happens in the most realistic setting, the page as shown, and costs nothing in the run itself. The source repository's landing page may show an unreviewed drawing between the push and the review. A rejection costs a further commit, or a revert followed by redoing the work, instead of a draft round. How long a weak drawing stays visible depends on whether a release falls within this mission, an axis a sibling question owns.

The maintainer supplies a rough sketch or reference of the arms (a coarse character layout, or a description of poses and curls), recorded in requirements.md before tasks are derived. The executing agent refines it into the final drawing at the decided size and character set, accepting the result on its own judgment by its faithfulness to the sketch. The composition, which is the part of the drawing taste decides most, comes from the maintainer. The agent does the laborious character-level work, and execution stays unattended once the sketch is recorded. The maintainer has to produce and record a sketch before tasks can be derived. Refining can still lose what made the sketch work, and nothing but the agent's own judgment checks that it did not.

The maintainer draws the finished character art and supplies it, recorded in requirements.md or handed over as a file before tasks are derived. The executing agent only places it, taking it verbatim, so the maintainer's authorship is the acceptance and no further judgment of the drawing is made. The drawing is exactly what the maintainer wants, with no draft rounds and no taste criteria to formulate. Execution afterwards is mechanical and unattended. All the drawing effort falls on the maintainer, and execution cannot begin until the drawing exists. A drawing made before the size, character-set, and arm-count questions settle may need redrawing to fit them, so its timing depends on those sibling axes.

The drawing is not drawn from scratch. The executing agent finds existing character art of octopus arms or tentacles under a licence compatible with the repository's LICENSE, then adapts it to the banner's requirements. It accepts the result against recorded criteria that include licence compatibility and any attribution the source requires. Starts from art someone has already made work visually. That lowers the risk of a weak original drawing without needing the maintainer to draw. Most published character art carries no clear licence, so finding a usable source is uncertain, and attribution may have to appear somewhere on or near the banner. Arms curling up from a bottom edge is a specific composition that existing art rarely matches, so adaptation may amount to redrawing anyway.

open-question.question: How is the banner's rendered appearance checked before it is committed, the repository holding no tool that renders an SVG: by rendering the file locally to an image that is inspected, by viewing it on GitHub after a push in both page themes, or by no rendering check beyond the file being a well-formed SVG?
open-question.alternative: Before the commit, the SVG is rendered locally to a PNG with a renderer already on the machine and not added to the repository (macOS's WebKit-based qlmanage thumbnailer or ImageMagick, both present here; no rsvg-convert, Inkscape, or cairosvg is installed), composited on GitHub's light and dark page background colours, and inspected; nothing is committed for the check, and no GitHub view is part of it. Catches a wrong look before anything lands, in a fast loop that costs no push and no new dependency, and the rendered PNG is something the executing agent can itself read as an image while it iterates on the drawing. A local renderer is not what a viewer's browser on GitHub draws: text elements fall back to this machine's fonts rather than the viewer's, and ImageMagick's own SVG renderer supports less than a browser does, so a banner can pass locally and still misrender on the page; how much that gap matters depends on how the characters are drawn (text versus outlined paths), which a sibling question settles, and whose eyes judge the PNG is the drawing-approval sibling's axis.

A small script committed under scripts/ renders the SVG to PNGs on the light and dark page backgrounds, run before each commit that touches the banner and inspected by eye; it is a tool run by hand, not a test, and no GitHub view is part of the check. The check is reproducible: any later edit of the banner, by anyone, re-renders it the same way rather than relying on whatever renderer happens to be installed. Adds a tool the repository does not have today, which either brings a rendering dependency into a tooling project whose one dependency is PyYAML or shells out to a platform-specific renderer, and it carries the same local-versus-GitHub fidelity gap as any local render while leaving one more file to maintain for an image that may rarely change.

The banner is committed on a scratch branch pushed to the source repository (or opened as a pull request), and the root README and each rendered hosts/<host>/README.md are viewed on github.com in both the light and dark page themes before the change lands on main; no local render is made. Checks the real thing before it is public on the landing page: GitHub's own image serving and sanitization, in a real browser, in both themes, exactly as a visitor will see it. Needs a push and a branch outside the mission's usual commit-on-main flow, every fix costs another push-and-look round, and an unattended executing agent cannot view the page itself, so the look is judged by whoever opens the browser; a host README's relative image path resolves on the source repository's branch only if the delivery chosen by a sibling question places the file there.

The banner is committed on main as any other change, with no rendering check before the commit; once pushed, the root README and the rendered host READMEs are viewed on github.com in both page themes, and anything wrong is corrected by a follow-up commit. Fits the workflow as it runs, one commit per task on main with no extra branch or tool, while still checking the true rendered look on the page that matters. Rejects the "before it is committed" premise: a misrendered banner is public on the source repository's landing page until the fix lands, and it would ride into a release if the push-and-look step is skipped before one, which a sibling question decides whether this mission makes.

The SVG is rendered locally to PNGs on the light and dark backgrounds and inspected before the commit, with a renderer already on the machine and nothing committed for it, and after the push to main the README pages are viewed on github.com in both themes as a final confirmation, a fix landing as a follow-up commit. Combines a fast pre-commit loop that catches most mistakes before they are public with a final check against what visitors actually see, covering the local renderer's fidelity gap. The most effort of any option, two checks for one image, and a fault only GitHub shows still reaches the public page briefly before its follow-up fix.

No rendering check at all: the SVG is checked only to parse as well-formed XML and its source read to confirm its colours and dimensions are the ones decided; the rendered look is never inspected before or after the commit. Costs nothing beyond what any committed file gets and needs no renderer, push, or human viewing, so an unattended execution can complete it end to end. The banner exists only to look right, and nothing confirms it does: fallback fonts misaligning the art, colours unreadable on one theme, or a wrong displayed size all ship unseen; the risk is lower only if the characters are outlined as paths, which a sibling question decides.

open-question.question: What alternative text does the banner image carry in the four READMEs: an empty alt marking the image as decorative, or a short description of the arms, and in that case what wording?
open-question.alternative: The banner's image element carries no alt attribute at all in any of the four READMEs: no text is written for it, empty or otherwise, and what a screen reader or a failed image load shows is left to the browser. Nothing to word or keep in step across the four files, so the banner's line in each README is the shortest it can be. Breaks the pattern every image on the four pages follows today, each badge carrying a written alt such as "Latest Release" or "unique views"; screen readers commonly announce the file name or URL in its place, and a broken load shows nothing that says what was meant to be there.

The banner carries an empty alt (alt="") in all four READMEs, marking it as decorative so assistive technology skips it and the page's spoken reading starts at the badges, then the title. Matches what the banner is for a non-sighted reader: pure ornament ahead of a title that already names the project, so nothing redundant is read before the "# Gurita" heading, and no wording has to track the drawing's arm count, characters, or colours as those are settled or later changed. A sighted reader whose image fails to load, and every screen-reader user, learns nothing of the banner at all; it is also the one image on the pages with no written alt, so the choice reads as an omission unless it is understood as deliberate.

The banner carries one short literal description of the picture, identical in all four READMEs, naming only what is drawn and how, with no colours and no counts — for example "Octopus arms drawn in ASCII art" — and nothing of the project's name or tagline. Tells anyone who cannot see the image what is there in a few words, follows the written-alt pattern the badges already set, and stays true whatever arm count, size, or palette the sibling questions settle, so it needs no rewording when the drawing is tuned. Read aloud before the title on every page, it adds a line a screen-reader user hears ahead of the project's name for an image that conveys no information; the words "ASCII art" hold only while the art's character set is limited to ASCII, which the art-character-set question decides.

The banner carries one fuller literal description, identical in all four READMEs, stating what is drawn, how it sits, and its colours — for example "Octopus arms curling up from the bottom edge, drawn in violet and grey-blue characters" — still naming neither the project nor the tagline. Gives a non-sighted reader or a failed load the closest equivalent of the picture, its shape and its palette included, which is the whole of what the banner adds to the pages. The longest text read ahead of the title on every page, and every detail it names (the colours, the curling from the bottom edge, any count) becomes a fact the alt must keep in step with the drawing by hand in four files; its wording depends on how the palette, arm count, and character-set questions are settled.

The banner carries the project's name as its alt in all four READMEs — "Gurita" in each, treating the banner as the project's logo — with no description of the arms. Follows the common convention for a header image standing in as a logo, needs no wording to track the drawing's details, and gives a failed load a sensible label. Each page's next heading already says "Gurita" ("# Gurita" or "# Gurita for <Host>"), so a screen reader hears the name twice in a row, and the text says nothing of what the image shows.

The banner carries the tagline "Decide first, then let the arms carry the work." as its alt in all four READMEs, describing the image by the metaphor it illustrates rather than by its appearance. Ties the picture to the meaning the earlier rename mission gave the arms, so a reader who cannot see the banner still gets what it stands for, and it brings that line to the three host pages, which carry no tagline today. On the root README the same sentence stands as bold text just under the title, so it is read twice there; on the host pages it adds the tagline the finished rename mission deliberately kept off them, and it does not say what the image actually depicts.

open-question.question: Does this mission include a release that publishes the banner to the three host landing pages, which change only when a release publishes the host trees, or does it end with the banner committed on main, showing only on the source repository's page until the next release?

Is the host suite run on all three hosts as part of this mission, since adding the banner to each host's README template changes every host's trigger set and the suite first requires each host's installed copy to equal the built tree, or is that run left to the next release's pre-flight?

Does a permanent check guard the banner once it is in place, for example a test that each of the four READMEs opens with the banner image or that every committed copy of the SVG is identical, or is the banner verified once when its tasks are completed, no test reading a README's content today?
